prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, enabling measurement of time and frequency at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep the single-part configuration B048, crediting Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye, and I have not changed it since round 1. After the full exchange my reasons are firmer, not merely shared. The mechanism is unambiguous: a magic wavelength cancels the lattice light shift to first order while many neutral atoms sit in the Lamb-Dicke regime, so one gets Doppler- and recoil-free interrogation with the statistics of thousands of atoms. The performance near 1e-18 is reported from several laboratories and species, which is the independent confirmation I ask of any result before I would call it established. And it has already produced physics rather than just a smaller error bar: millimetre-scale redshift, constraints on drifting constants and ultralight dark matter, and spin-exchange and other many-body effects inside the clock that look much like condensed-matter problems. This last point answers the chair's first question for me. The 2005 prize gave the field a frequency ruler and the 2012 prize gave control of single quantum systems; the lattice clock needs neither a comb nor a single ion to be what it is, and it rests on its own idea and its own systematic-error budget. The citation should therefore name the lattice clock and nothing broader, and I would keep the 10^-18 clause because it states the achievement quantitatively and avoids a vague metrology label. On the chair's second question, two names are defensible: Katori for the concept and first realisation, Ye for taking the system to record accuracy and to the many-body regime.
statement.case_against: The honest weakness is that this is an instrument and method advance, and members from outside atomic physics, myself included when I think as a condensed-matter theorist, can fairly ask whether it is a discovery of nature. I answer that mainly through the physics the clock has opened, but it is a judgement and not a proof. The second weakness is the chronology. All of us, I included, are working from memory for the order of Katori's 2003 proposal, the first strontium lattice-clock measurements and the later record uncertainties. Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Boyd and Hollberg have real roles, and I cannot show from the supplied text that none of them should displace or join either named laureate. If the primary papers showed that someone other than Katori or Ye is the second decisive name, I would revisit the pair. I do not see that at present. The alternatives are weaker on this test: B019 has the deeper physics but an unresolved credit set (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu, Moore) and overlaps the 2016 topology prize, and B036 has an open mechanism question and device-dependent reproducibility.

responses.point: You put the clock first, test it against the charge that it is the second discoverer doing it better, and conclude that it is a distinct invention because the magic wavelength does not follow from the comb or from ion traps. You also say you may be undervaluing the Higgs case and ask for the 2003 to 2005 priority to be checked.
responses.response: I accept your test and your answer. The magic-wavelength condition is a different physical idea with its own error budget, so I do not think it is a refinement of the 2012 work. On priority, I agree it needs checking and cannot do it from primary papers here, so I would ask anyone with the 2003 to 2005 record to say if it contradicts the Katori-first account. As for the Higgs, I do not think you undervalue it scientifically, but I share the objection you raise: until the committee has a rule that picks three names from four across ATLAS and CMS, B054 is not a ballot I can support, and I would not want to improvise one at the last stage.

responses.point: You say the clock combines an original idea, a decisive experiment and broad confirmation, and that the strongest reservation is distinctness from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, which is a judgement and not a fact. You also say you cannot settle Katori versus Ye weighting from memory.
responses.response: I agree that distinctness is a judgement and I hold it with that label. I would put it differently from my round-1 wording, though: the test is whether the prize could be written without invoking the comb or the single ion, and it can, since the citation turns on a lattice of neutral atoms at a magic wavelength. On the credit split, I would not treat Katori versus Ye as a ranking problem. The two contributions are complementary, concept plus first realisation and record performance plus many-body control, and neither alone would give a complete prize. Your caution about memory is correct, and you are better placed than I am to say whether the 2003 proposal and the first Sr lattice clock support Katori's position.

responses.point: You are comfortable with the clock first, but you list timing relative to the SI redefinition as a concern and say that dropping either Katori or Ye would worry you more than the split between them.
responses.response: On timing I now join those who say not to wait. Last round I listed it as open; on reflection a prize for the invention and development of the lattice clock is justified by what has been demonstrated and reproduced, and does not depend on a decision by the metrology bodies. Waiting adds attribution risk as the field grows, which Kroll also noted. I agree with your point on the two names: they should stay together, and the citation should not split them by task. I would only keep my earlier point that the ion-clock and Yb and Hg communities are acknowledged in the background text, not in the credit.

responses.point: You say the clock is reproduced across laboratories and species, and that many-body spin-exchange physics inside it is a research topic in its own right; you also decline B025 as a second prize part.
responses.response: I agree on both points. The many-body physics is what persuades me that the clock is a physics result and not only a metrology one, and I would say so in the citation or its background. On a second part, I considered whether anything would complete the configuration, and I do not find a credit set that fits in the one remaining name. B025 would need Bordé, Pritchard and Kasevich plus Katori and Ye, five names against a limit of three, and B019 would need more names than that. A single part with two laureates is the better configuration than a second part with a contested credit.

uncertainties: Whether the full committee regards the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; I judge it distinct but this is a judgement.

The exact chronology of Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, the first strontium lattice-clock demonstrations and the record accuracy results, which I am still taking from memory and from colleagues and not from the primary papers; a documented claim by Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Boyd or Hollberg could change the credit.
Whether two names are enough given the breadth of the lattice-clock community, and whether the citation as worded is narrow enough.

Whether B019 or B036 would be better in a later year once credit (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu, Moore) or mechanism (twisted bilayer graphene) questions are settled; I do not think either is ready now.
statement.conflict_note: No specific tie to Katori, Ye, or the other lattice-clock groups. For transparency, I chaired the 2025 committee that awarded the superconducting-circuit prize, which bears on how I view B001 (circuit QED) if it returns, and I would be cautious about supporting it so soon after. My DFT and spin-dynamics work for MAX IV and ESS is a general field connection to condensed-matter candidates such as B019 and B036, not a personal tie to any named candidate. I do not think any disclosed flag among the members, including Johansson on B001, Olsson's Tokyo fellowship and Kroll's Boulder year, requires recusal from the B048-only configuration, though that is for the chair to rule.
